```{r, include = FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(collapse = TRUE, comment = "#>")
```

```{r setup}
library(zuregex)
```

We take a few lines of a web server's log and work through them: find the
lines that match, pull out parts of them, turn them into a data frame,
rewrite them and cut them up. After that you know the main `re_*()`
functions and the rules they share. Moving from base R or stringr, limits
on untrusted patterns and the C API each have their own article, listed
at the end.

## Detect matches

The log is a character vector. Its last element is not a log line, so we
can see what a string that does not match gives.

```{r}
log <- c(
  "2026-10-21 08:15:02 GET /index.html 200 512",
  "2026-10-21 08:15:09 POST /login 302 0",
  "2026-10-21 08:16:44 GET /missing 404 128",
  "not a log line"
)
```

Every function takes the strings first, as `x`, and then a **pattern**: a
regular expression in PCRE2's syntax, which is the syntax of base R's
`perl = TRUE`. `re_detect()` says which elements match.

```{r}
re_detect(log, "GET")
```

One pattern is used for every element. The other choice is one pattern per
element, as long as `x`. Here each line is tested for its own status code,
and only the second line has the one asked for.

```{r}
re_detect(log, c("404", "302", "200", "500"))
```

A pattern of any other length is an error: zuregex never recycles one.

## Extract matches

`re_extract()` returns the text of the first match in each element, and
`NA` where there is none.

```{r}
re_extract(log, "/\\S+")
```

Parentheses in a pattern make a **group**, a part of the match you can ask
for by itself. `group` picks one, by number or, for a group written
`(?<name>...)`, by name. This returns the status code alone, without the
spaces the pattern needs around it.

```{r}
re_extract(log, " (?<status>\\d{3}) ", group = "status")
```

## Capture groups as columns

`re_match()` returns every group at once, as a data frame with one row per
element. A named group gives its name to its column.

```{r}
pattern <- "(?<time>\\S+ \\S+) (?<method>[A-Z]+) (?<path>\\S+) (?<status>\\d+)"
re_match(log, pattern)
```

The columns are character. `proto` gives them types, as it does for
`utils::strcapture()`: a data frame whose columns are examples of the type
wanted. Look at `status`, now an integer.

```{r}
proto <- data.frame(time = "", method = "", path = "", status = 0L)
str(re_match(log, pattern, proto = proto))
```

`re_match()` looks at the first match in each element. `re_match_all()`
returns a row for every match, with `element` and `match` saying where each
came from. Each of the first three lines has two numbers at its end, and
the last line has no rows.

```{r}
re_match_all(log, " (?<number>\\d+)(?= |$)")
```

## Replace and split

`re_replace()` replaces every match with a **template**, in which
`${name}` or `$1` stands for a group. Here the date is turned round, and
the line with no date comes back unchanged.

```{r}
re_replace(log, "^(?<y>\\d+)-(?<m>\\d+)-(?<d>\\d+)", "${d}/${m}/${y}")
```

Templates can do more than this, such as defaults and case changes;
`?re_replace` lists the syntax.

`re_split()` cuts each element at the matches, and returns a list with a
character vector of pieces per element.

```{r}
re_split(log[1:2], " ")
```

## Compile a pattern once

So far each pattern was a string. `re_compile()` turns one into an **`re`
object**, which carries its flags with it and which every function takes
in place of the string. The flag `i` ignores case, so this lower-case
pattern finds the log's `GET`.

```{r}
get <- re_compile("\\bget\\b", flags = "i")
get
re_detect(log, get)
```

You do not need `re_compile()` for speed. Pattern strings go through a
cache, so a string used again is not compiled again; see `?re_cache_size`.

## When a pattern is wrong

The most common mistake is a pattern that is not valid. This one never
closes the group it opens.

```{r, error = TRUE}
re_match(log, "(?<time>\\S+ \\S+ (?<method>[A-Z]+)")
```

The error names the problem and marks where in the pattern PCRE2 found it.
Like every error zuregex raises, it has a class, here
`zuregex_error_compile`, so `tryCatch()` can handle it.

## Where next

* [Move from base R and stringr](https://pedrobtz.github.io/zuregex/articles/from-base-r.html)
  maps the functions you know onto these, and shows what behaves
  differently.
* [Bound the work of a match](https://pedrobtz.github.io/zuregex/articles/limits.html)
  is for patterns or input you do not trust.
* [Link to zuregex from C](https://pedrobtz.github.io/zuregex/articles/c-api.html)
  uses the same PCRE2 from another package's C code.
* [Design and motivation](https://pedrobtz.github.io/zuregex/articles/design.html)
  explains why zuregex exists next to base R's own PCRE2, and what it
  leaves out.
* The [reference index](https://pedrobtz.github.io/zuregex/reference/)
  lists every function, including the ones this page skipped: counting,
  locating, escaping, and the thread and cache controls.
